title: Najdorf: when it goes wrong and how to repair it
outcomes: Names three typical Black mistakes in the Najdorf (a pawn grab with the king at home, a pawn move while pieces sleep, a slow move in a race) and two White ones (ignoring a pin, retreating when a pawn push counters) with the engine's verdict on each
Finds the repair at the moment of the mistake (...Be7, ...b4, Bg3, e5) and the least bad move afterwards (...Rc8, c3)
Says when ...Qxb2 holds and when ...Qxc2 fails, using a stated rule of thumb and its exception
Reads a scan of 250 games with its sample size and depth, and says what it does not show
sources: library/data/games (TWIC weekly PGN zips, 2012 to 2026): games filtered by script (both players 2550+, first ten plies 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 a6); real mistakes taken from Hovhannisyan - Gabuzyan (Lake Sevan, 24 Jul 2016, 1-0), Dubov - Sjugirov (19th European Individual Championship, 27 Mar 2018, 0-1), Hou Yifan - Van Wely (78th Tata Steel Group A, 24 Jan 2016, 0-1), Saric - Shirov (20th European Team Championship, 17 Nov 2015, 1-0) and Caruana - Vachier-Lagrave (83rd Tata Steel Masters, 23 Jan 2021, 1-0); moves and results checked with python-chess [V]. Moves and results are facts; every comment is our own wording

Scan of 250 decisive classical games (both players 2600+, TWIC issues 1001 to 1257, 2014 to 2018, the first 250 of 616 such games in file order), Stockfish 19 lite at depth 12 on plies 11 to 52; a swing is a drop of at least 130 centipawns in one move from a position with |eval| under 400; 59 games had one, first at move 15 or earlier in 7, moves 16 to 20 in 17 and moves 21 to 26 in 35, and the side that made it lost in 47 [V]; depth 12 is noisy and the sample is small

steps.text: **The question.** The Najdorf is a sharp opening, and sharp openings punish small slips. What do strong players actually get wrong, and how do they repair it? You will meet three kinds of Black mistake and two of White's. Some positions are from real games between players rated above 2,550; the ...h6 and ...Ne8 examples are engine suggestions, labelled as such. Each comes with the engine's check and the repair. Then you will sort new positions.

steps.text: **A rule with an exception.** Nimzowitsch, in *My System*, wrote: "Never play to win a pawn while your development is yet unfinished!" [V-quote: citable-views 1.7]. He allowed an exception for a central pawn taken without great danger. That is a rule of thumb, and rules of thumb have conditions. The next position is a pawn grab that strong players choose again and again, on the wing and with development unfinished. Watch what is different.

steps.prompt: Predict for each edited position whether the grab ...Qxc2 is a good move, then check. One difference matters, and one does not.

steps.text: **What separates the grabs?** [V] In the same position, ...Qxc2 loses about a pawn and a half while Black's king is at home and f7 is weak. Once the bishop is on e7 and the king has castled, the grab is the engine's first choice. A pawn move on the other wing changes nothing. [H] Three questions may tell grabs apart: can my queen get home, how many pieces still sleep, can I catch up with White's attack? These fit a few positions; they are not laws.

steps.text: **Count the sleepers.** Edward Lasker, in *Chess Strategy*, taught that a lead in development licenses a direct attack and that a deficit voids it [V-sheet: citable-views 4.9]. [I] Black's ...h6 and ...d5 spend a tempo while three pieces sleep. [H] A rule to test: before a pawn move with more than two pieces asleep, ask whether it develops or defends. Check pawn moves too: at depth 16 even ...b5 is close, at depth 18 it falls behind.

steps.text: **Slow in a race.** [V] With the best reply (...b4) White stands at about +0.3 to +0.6; after ...Ne8 or ...h5 it is about +1.8 to +2.7. The same idea as before, from another angle: in an opposite-wing race, Black's moves must hit White's king or White's best square. [H] Counterplay that is one tempo late is the same as no counterplay. Whether one tempo matters depends on who is closer to the other king.

steps.text: **Repair, don't panic.** Znosko-Borovsky (*The Middle Game in Chess*) advised diagnosing your chief weakness and the opponent's chief threat, then defending with a long plan rather than one threat at a time [V-sheet: citable-views 5.4]. Here the diagnosis is a pin on the d4 knight; the quiet repair adds a defender. [I] The two desperado moves are what players choose when they do not diagnose.

steps.text: **How often, and when?** I ran the engine (depth 12) over 250 decisive classical Najdorf games, both players 2,600 or more, 2014 to 2018 [V]. In 59 games (24%) a side lost at least 1.3 pawns in one move: 7 by move 15, 17 in moves 16 to 20, 35 in moves 21 to 26. That side then lost 47 times. Caveats: the scan stops at move 26, every game was decisive (so about half of them were lost by chance), and depth 12 is shallow.

steps.text:
**Recap.**
- Black: a grab with king and rooks at home loses about a pawn and a half; with a safe queen retreat it is the engine's choice. [V]
- Black: develop when pieces sleep; in a race, hit the king or d5. [V, H]
- White: do not ignore a pin; push when a push counters. [V]
- Repair: diagnose, add a defender. [I]
